claims.text: The baseline is a W–Cu composite with uncoated tungsten particles and typical W–Cu interfacial thermal resistance.
Tungsten particles will be coated with a nanocrystalline W–Ta–Cr–V–Hf RHEA before copper infiltration.
The coating will form a uniform nanocrystalline RHEA layer at the W–Cu interface.
The interfacial RHEA layer will promote metallurgical bonding between tungsten and copper.
The interfacial RHEA layer will minimize defects at the W–Cu interface.
A structurally coherent RHEA transition between tungsten and copper will reduce interfacial thermal resistance.
Nanocrystalline WTaCrVHf RHEA has high thermal stability under extreme environments.
Nanocrystalline WTaCrVHf RHEA is resistant to heavy-ion irradiation, dual-beam irradiation, and helium implantation.
The RHEA coating will reduce irradiation-induced defect accumulation in the coated W–Cu composite.
The RHEA coating will help maintain the mechanical integrity of the W–Cu composite under irradiation.
The coated W–Cu composite will have higher overall thermal conductivity than an otherwise comparable uncoated W–Cu composite.
The coated composite will retain mechanical strength comparable to the uncoated composite.
The coated composite will retain irradiation resistance comparable to the uncoated composite.
The predicted improvement requires a continuous, defect-free interfacial coating.
Poor coating-thickness control, nonuniformity, or deleterious interfacial reactions may limit the improvement.
The quantitative thermal-conductivity improvement and long-term stability of the RHEA–Cu interface under fusion-reactor conditions have not been validated.
